Molluscum contagiosum is highly likely given its classic appearance (pearly, umbilicated papules), common abdominal involvement (especially in children/immunocompetent adults via autoinoculation or fomite exposure), and lack of symptoms. Keratosis pilaris is plausible though typically more common on extensor surfaces (arms/thighs); truncal involvement occurs, especially in darker skin types, and it can be asymptomatic. Small superficial epidermal inclusion cysts may present as discrete, mobile, flesh-colored papules—less common on abdomen but possible after minor trauma. Steatocystoma multiplex is a rare autosomal dominant condition featuring multiple small, soft, yellowish cysts, often beginning in adolescence/early adulthood on trunk/abdomen; less common but fits morphology and location. Lichen nitidus is uncommon, presenting as tiny, flat-topped, skin-colored papules, often asymptomatic and sometimes clustered on abdomen—but typically more uniform in size and associated with subtle scale or luster; lower confidence due to rarity and frequent association with other inflammatory dermatoses. Absence of systemic symptoms, inflammation, scaling, or pruritus makes infectious (e.g., secondary syphilis), inflammatory (e.g., guttate psoriasis), or malignant entities much less likely."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Milia", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Steatocystoma multiplex", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Vellus hair cyst", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Epidermoid cyst (small, superficial, non-inflamed)", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Flat warts (verruca plana)", "confidence": 0.55}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "The presentation—multiple small, painless, non-itchy, asymptomatic abdominal bumps in an otherwise healthy individual—strongly favors benign, epidermal or follicular-derived cystic lesions. Milia (keratin-filled eccrine ductal cysts) are highly likely given their classic appearance as 1–2 mm firm, white-to-yellow papules, often on trunk/face, and lack of expression upon gentle pressure (consistent with absence of expressed material). Steatocystoma multiplex is plausible due to its typical truncal distribution, multiple small-to-medium cystic papules, and occasional expression of oily/sebaceous material—but the absence of reported expression lowers confidence slightly. Vellus hair cysts share similar morphology and location but often contain laminated keratin and vellus hairs; they may be subtle and underrecognized. Small epidermoid cysts can present similarly but usually have a more central punctum and firmer, cheesy core—if expression were observed, confidence would rise; its current absence makes it less likely but still possible. Flat warts are less likely: they are typically flesh-colored or brown, slightly scaly, and more common on hands/face; they do not express material and are rarely described as 'bumps' on abdomen without associated viral stigmata (e.g., koebnerization, periungual spread), hence lower confidence."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Milia", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Steatocystoma multiplex", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Verruca plana", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Epidermoid cyst (small, superficial, non-inflamed)", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Fibrous papule of the skin", "confidence": 0.58}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.542, "reasoning": "The presentation—multiple small, painless, nonpruritic, non-inflammatory papules on the abdomen in a child—is highly characteristic of milia (keratin-filled epidermal cysts), especially primary milia in children, which commonly arise spontaneously on the trunk and face without trauma or systemic association; confidence is high (0.92) given absence of inflammation, discharge, scaling, or sun-exposure pattern. Steatocystoma multiplex is plausible (0.78) as it presents with multiple asymptomatic, smooth, flesh-colored to yellowish cystic papules/nodules, often on the trunk—but typically emerges in adolescence/early adulthood and is less common in young children; still included due to classic cystic appearance and lack of inflammation. Epidermoid cysts (0.72) are considered because they may present as small, firm, asymptomatic papules, though they more commonly occur in teens/adults and usually have a visible punctum—less typical in young children without expression history. Verruca plana (0.65) is included cautiously: although typically slightly scaly and sometimes clustered, some flat warts can appear minimally elevated and asymptomatic on the trunk, but absence of hyperkeratosis, koebnerization, or spread makes it less likely. Fibrous papule (0.58) is the least likely: it is almost exclusively solitary, occurs on the nose/face in adults, and is firm and dome-shaped—not consistent with multiple abdominal papules in a child. Excluded: molluscum (would have central umbilication and often pruritus or clustering), keratosis pilaris (scaly, folliculocentric, upper arms/thighs), xanthomas (associated with dyslipidemia, yellow-orange hue), and nevi (usually present at birth or early infancy, not newly noticed en masse)."}
